title: Extraction in red wines
subtitle: Colour, tannin and flavour
objectives: Explain cold soak and extended maceration

steps.title: Before, during, after
steps.body: Extraction can happen before fermentation, as cold soak, where crushed grapes sit cool for days to draw out colour and fruit in water, not alcohol. During fermentation, cap management does the work. After fermentation, extended maceration keeps wine on skins for days or weeks, softening and polymerising tannins.
steps.highlight: Cold soak, cap management, extended maceration

steps.title: Temperature and tannin
steps.body: Alcohol dissolves tannin more easily than water, so most tannin is extracted later in fermentation. Higher temperatures, 28 to 32 degrees, extract more. Extended maceration, often used for Bordeaux and Barolo, lets short tannins bind into longer chains, which feel softer on the palate.

steps.prompt: Why is a cold soak done before fermentation?
options: To extract colour and fruit without much tannin
steps.explanation: Cold soak happens in water, not alcohol, so it extracts colour and fruit aromas but little tannin.

steps.title: Whole bunches
steps.body: Some winemakers ferment with whole bunches, stems included. Part of the fermentation happens inside intact berries, giving fresh, floral, spicy notes. Ripe stems add tannin and structure and can lower colour and acidity slightly. It is common in Burgundy, the northern Rhône and among many modern producers of Pinot Noir and Syrah.

steps.prompt: Match each technique to its timing.
steps.explanation: Extraction is planned across the whole process.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Extraction happens before, during and after fermentation
Heat and alcohol extract more tannin
Whole bunches add freshness, spice and structure
